profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a university-affiliated research computing institute that wants to design a small pilot program inspired by a recent paper on testing research software. The institute supports faculty labs whose code ranges from polished Python packages to one-off analysis scripts used in publications, and leadership has asked for 3-4 concrete intervention ideas that could improve testing habits without creating heavy process overhead. The agenda is to generate candidate approaches for next semester, screen them for plausibility, and leave with an aligned-looking shortlist to draft into a one-page pilot concept note. The expected outcome is not a final implementation plan, but a shared-seeming set of promising ideas such as templates, training, guidance, and support structures.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Scientific Python tooling, CI/CD for computational workflows, repository standardization, reproducibility infrastructure
members.background: Nina leads a small central RSE team that helps campus research groups turn prototype code into maintainable software, especially by setting up packaging, automated checks, and reusable repository patterns for Python-based projects.
members.private_state: She wants pilot ideas that can show visible improvement within one semester, fit within her team's limited support capacity, and lean on reusable infrastructure rather than high-touch consulting with each lab.
hidden_assumptions: When people ask for 'testing templates,' they usually mean reusable repository templates with pre-wired pytest, CI workflows, and example test files that a team can copy directly.

If the institute wants to standardize practices across teams, the realistic path is to standardize on a supported toolchain boundary first, especially GitHub-hosted Python repositories already under central support.
A minimal testing bar only counts if checks run automatically and repeatedly, because manual validation tends to decay once students graduate or deadlines hit.
Calls for a 'culture change' around testing are mainly about normalizing modern engineering habits such as pull requests, CI, and routine automated checks in research code.

members.name: Dr. Omar Haddad
members.expertise: Scientific modeling workflows, lab software practices, faculty adoption, mentoring student developers
members.background: Omar is a computational biology faculty member who sits on the institute's software practices committee and often translates engineering recommendations into forms that principal investigators, postdocs, and graduate students will accept in everyday research work.
members.private_state: He wants any pilot to feel legitimate to faculty labs with messy real-world workflows, to avoid implying that good scientific practice requires everyone to migrate tools, and to make testing feel compatible with publication-driven research rather than imported from industry.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'testing templates,' they usually mean adaptable documents and examples: lab checklists, manuscript-release guidance, and sample validation cases that can be used regardless of language or hosting platform.

If the institute wants to standardize practices across teams, it should standardize expectations and norms, not require common infrastructure, because many important projects live on private servers, in R or MATLAB, or as mixed-language workflows.
A minimal testing bar can be satisfied by documented scientific validation on representative cases before release or publication, even if parts of that process are manual.

Calls for a 'culture change' around testing are mainly about changing local incentives and mentoring norms so faculty and trainees treat testing as part of credible science rather than optional engineering polish.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that providing 'testing templates' would make adoption easier for research groups.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means repository-level templates such as a GitHub template repo with pytest configured, a .github/workflows/test.yml file, coverage setup, and a few sample unit and regression tests.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means process and documentation templates such as a lab testing checklist, a manuscript code-release checklist, and domain-oriented examples of validation cases teams can adapt in any environment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'templates' feels fully specified and broadly inclusive, so each person assumes the other is endorsing their natural interpretation rather than hearing it as a term needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'standardize practices across teams'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the institute should try to 'standardize practices across teams' rather than create something niche.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means converging teams onto a common supported implementation pattern, effectively standardizing the tooling layer for the subset of projects on the institute's GitHub organization, mainly Python repositories using centrally managed CI.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means establishing shared expectations that apply across heterogeneous environments, including R scripts on lab servers, MATLAB models, and mixed-language pipelines that may never move into the central GitHub organization.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a harmless aspiration toward consistency, and both hear it as plainly desirable; the disagreement lies in the invisible boundary between standardizing tools versus standardizing norms.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both use the phrase 'baseline tests' when discussing the minimum bar a pilot should encourage.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes baseline tests means automated smoke tests plus a small number of deterministic regression checks that run in CI on every pull request or at least on every merge to main.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes baseline tests means a documented set of scientifically meaningful validation cases, such as reproducing expected outputs on 3-5 canonical datasets before a paper submission or major release, whether or not those checks are automated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because 'baseline' sounds intentionally modest, both hear it as a practical middle ground and do not probe the operational threshold for what actually counts as having met the baseline.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both invoke the need for a 'culture change' around testing when justifying pilot ideas.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes 'culture change' to mean researchers adopting routine engineering behaviors: opening pull requests instead of pushing directly, keeping test folders in repos, and expecting CI to run automatically before code changes are accepted.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes 'culture change' to mean faculty and trainees treating testing as part of scientific credibility: budgeting time for validation, discussing test evidence in lab meetings, and rewarding students for building checks even when no new feature is shipped.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At a high level both interpretations are positive and mutually compatible-sounding, so references to 'culture change' create strong false consensus even though each person imagines a different mechanism of change.

turns.inner_thought: That paper basically matches what our team sees: people are not anti-testing, they just need a practical starting point. I need to keep this anchored to something we can show within one semester and support with reusable infrastructure, not a consulting-heavy program for every lab. If I frame it broadly enough, we can still steer toward the Python repos already under central support.
turns.utterance: I thought the survey paper was useful because it confirmed that most groups already believe testing matters; the sticking point is practical support. So for today, I'd like us to focus on a small pilot we could actually run next semester, not a giant strategy exercise.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but the pilot has to feel like ordinary research practice, not imported bureaucracy. What matters to faculty is whether this sounds connected to credible science, publication readiness, and student training. That's the culture change I want us to aim for.
turns.utterance: That sounds right. And I think whatever we put forward should help labs treat testing as part of normal research work rather than something added at the very end. If it nudges a real culture change, it will be much easier for people to take seriously.

turns.inner_thought: A template repo is the cleanest intervention: prewired pytest, CI, coverage, and example tests that groups can copy with minimal help. That's exactly the kind of low-touch asset my team can maintain and roll out quickly. I'll just call them testing templates and let that do the work.
turns.utterance: One low-friction option would be to provide testing templates. That gives teams something usable immediately instead of asking every lab to invent its own setup from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, templates would help most if they show students and postdocs what acceptable practice looks like in a lab setting: a checklist, a release guide, example validation cases. People often need a repeatable model of what counts as good enough, and that naturally connects to baseline tests.
turns.utterance: I like that direction. Testing templates would be especially helpful for new students and postdocs, because they often need a repeatable way to learn what good enough looks like. If the entry point is concrete, baseline tests will feel much less intimidating.

turns.inner_thought: If leadership wants institute-level impact, we cannot build something bespoke for every group. The only scalable path is to standardize around a common supported pattern so our docs, onboarding, and support all line up. In practice that means a shared tooling boundary, even if I don't say that out loud.
turns.utterance: Exactly. And if we want the institute to see real impact, I think we should try to standardize practices across teams rather than create something niche. Otherwise support and onboarding get reinvented every single time.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with standardizing, but in my mind that means shared expectations across very different lab realities, not one common infrastructure. It has to feel legitimate to labs with messy workflows, older code, and mixed environments, even if I keep that implicit here.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree with that. If we can standardize practices across teams, people are much more likely to feel there are shared expectations instead of each lab guessing on its own.

turns.inner_thought: We need a crisp minimum bar or this turns into vague encouragement. For me that means a small number of automated checks that run routinely, because anything manual will disappear as soon as deadlines pile up. I'll keep it high-level and call them baseline tests.
turns.utterance: Another thing that could help is defining baseline tests for pilot participants. If the expectation is concrete but still lightweight, I think more groups would actually be willing to try it.

turns.inner_thought: Faculty will accept a minimum bar if it's framed scientifically: show the code behaves sensibly on a few representative cases before a submission or release. It doesn't need to sound like software compliance. That's what baseline tests should mean if we want broad uptake.
turns.utterance: I think faculty would respond well to that, especially if baseline tests are framed around checking a few representative scientific cases before results are shared publicly. That feels credible without sounding heavy.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If we can make testing part of the normal workflow, we can normalize better engineering habits: routine checks, more disciplined changes, less chaos when student code lands on our desks. That's the culture change worth pursuing from my side.
turns.utterance: Right, and ideally the pilot would also contribute to a broader culture change by making testing part of the routine workflow, not something only the most mature projects do.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but the message to PIs has to be about trustworthy science and mentoring. If they start treating test evidence as part of lab practice and student training, the behavior will stick. That's the culture change I care about, even if Nina hears it differently.
turns.utterance: I completely agree. And I think we'll need language and examples that help PIs see testing as integral to trustworthy science and to student training, not just an optional refinement.

turns.inner_thought: This is shaping into a manageable package: a reusable starter, a short guide for the minimum expectation, and a brief onboarding piece. If we recruit a few willing groups that are already close to our support model, we can deliver visible progress in one semester without overextending the team.
turns.utterance: So maybe the pilot is a bundle: testing templates, a short guide to baseline tests, and a brief onboarding component so a few willing groups can try the whole package first.

turns.inner_thought: That gives me enough to pitch this as light-touch and relevant to ordinary lab work. I can identify a few faculty who would try something framed around shared expectations and better local norms. Nina can probably flesh out the practical support side in her own way.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's a strong bundle. Why don't we each identify a few candidate labs and then draft a one-page note explaining how the pilot could standardize practices across teams while also nudging culture change? That should be enough to get leadership's reaction.
